name: gradient-methods-v1
description: EVA's MRI gradient-correction methods on locked-clock simulated recordings with known ground truth. Every arm sees the identical recording for a given seed, so arms are compared by within-seed difference rather than by their separate averages. Two scenarios differ in one parameter: `gradient-locked` carries the scenario file's 10% slow amplitude modulation, `gradient-steady` sets it to zero. That pair is the experiment: a local donor-neighbourhood template can track drifting artifact amplitude and a global average template cannot, so if the gap between those two engine families collapses when the modulation is removed, the gap is amplitude tracking rather than a defect. Moosmann is deliberately absent: it averages donor volumes by realignment-parameter similarity, and motion parameters are an external file that a headless replay cannot supply, so a Moosmann arm would silently fall back to unweighted averaging and report a number that is not Moosmann's.

scenarios.description: Zero EEG/MRI clock drift, gradient artifact only, no BCG, no ocular activity, no recording defects, and the scenario file's 10% slow amplitude modulation left in place. Chosen first because its best attainable score is known analytically rather than merely observed, which gives the harness itself a leakage check.

Identical to gradient-locked with the slow amplitude modulation removed. The only difference between the two scenarios, so any change in the ranking between them is attributable to amplitude drift and nothing else.

methods.label: No correction
methods.note: The generated recording, scored unchanged. Every other row in the table is an improvement over this one, and without it none of them can be read.

methods.label: MAR

methods.label: wAAS
methods.citation: Goldman, R. I., Stern, J. M., Engel, J., & Cohen, M. S. (2000). Acquiring simultaneous EEG and functional MRI. Clinical Neurophysiology, 111(11), 1974-1980. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1388-2457(00)00456-9
methods.note: Exponentially distance-weighted donors, so its effective donor count is below the nominal one. sqrt(N+1) remains a valid upper bound, not a target.

methods.label: wAAR
methods.citation: Goldman et al. (2000) template, least-squares scaled before subtraction.

methods.label: FASTR
methods.citation: Niazy, R. K., Beckmann, C. F., Iannetti, G. D., Brady, J. M., & Smith, S. M. (2005). Removal of FMRI environment artifacts from EEG data using optimal basis sets. NeuroImage, 28(3), 720-737. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2005.06.067
methods.note: No analytic ceiling: the OBS residual fit is not an average over a known donor count, so no closed-form best case exists. Stating one would make the leakage check meaningless rather than stricter.

methods.label: FARM
methods.citation: van der Meer, J. N., Tijssen, M. A. J., Bour, L. J., van Rootselaar, A. F., & Nederveen, A. J. (2010). Robust EMG-fMRI artifact reduction for motion (FARM). Clinical Neurophysiology, 121(5), 766-776. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clinph.2009.12.035

methods.label: Allen IAR
methods.citation: Allen, P. J., Josephs, O., & Turner, R. (2000). A method for removing imaging artifact from continuous EEG recorded during functional MRI. NeuroImage, 12(2), 230-239. https://doi.org/10.1006/nimg.2000.0599
methods.note: Fixed running sections with correlation-gated template updates, so its template is not an N-donor average and has no closed-form ceiling.
